extracted.intended_audience: authors (fiction and creative non-fiction) writing character dialogue and authentic accents/dialects in English
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors on creating believable, readable character voices and dialects in English dialogue, covering transliteration, grammar, vocabulary, rhythm, audience, politics, and immersion. Emphasises choices (hinting vs full transliteration) and trade-offs for readership and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical short answer: Vivid over bland; hint at accent and dialect, but don’t overdo it
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid over bland every time. Hint at accent and dialect, but don’t overdo it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythm for the music of the voice. Use occasional lexis (words, vocabulary) for colour. Don’t fuss about spelling and punctuation. This is the short, practical rule-of-thumb to balance authenticity against readability and immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Accents give characters a distinctive life
rubrics_metrics.description: Accents make a character's voice stand out; a lively, distinctive voice is better than a bland one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all characters sound the same they'll be dull and hard to tell apart. Test whether characters can be identified by dialogue alone (a scriptwriting exercise). Example: rendering 'Southern' as 'Sudden' preserves character. Caveat: watch for overuse and the risk of caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Dialect and vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: You can evoke dialect by transliteration (spelling) or by using regional lexis/vocabulary to add colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle a few well-chosen dialect words to bring the world to life without overwhelming the reader. Provide enough context so unusual words are understandable (e.g., 'baloney' as food). Avoid overdoing transliteration; lexical colour plus context is often more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Regional accents also have distinct grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialect differences include grammar—not just pronunciation—and distinctive grammar can convey voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grammatical variants to create rhythm and authenticity (examples: 'what did you have for your tea?', 'Ain’t neither one of them', 'how it gits et'). Grammar can evoke voice without resorting to heavy spelling changes that impede readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. How you write an accent is political
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices about portraying non-standard language variants carry social and political implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many dialects have been stigmatized historically; choosing to portray them can support or challenge those power dynamics. Be aware that representing a non-standard dialect publicly is a statement and can contribute to preserving a language or culture—consider ethics and audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. An authentic voice doesn't need faithful transliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithful transliteration of dialect can be unreadable and pull readers out of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete transliteration may alienate general readers; a few hints and flavours usually suffice. Transliteration is a matter of degree (apologetic apostrophes vs glottal stops). Use readable cues rather than making text a 'code' to decode. Example: misguided phonetic renderings (e.g., KEERsher) can mislead pronunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Context and audience are crucial
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how strongly to render dialect based on your intended readership and market goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very faithful regional dialect may limit commercial appeal (likely suits small literary/regional/experimental markets). If your aim is a broad/global readership, compromise to capture flavour without alienating readers. Choose the degree of fidelity that aligns with who you want to reach and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Standard English doesn't exist
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Standard’ varieties are social constructs and idealized conventions rather than a single true form of English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding that 'standard' is created by social forces should free writers from hang-ups about non-standard variants. Standard forms have high status historically, but they are not inherently linguistically superior—use this to justify authentic voices where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Language keeps evolving
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is fluid; dictionaries give a static illusion but language mutates and communities create new words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers can invent words or reflect evolving usages—treat language playfully and creatively where it serves voice and story. Ensure invented or unusual forms make sense in context so they don't distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. There's no one correct way to write a voice
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no absolute rights and wrongs in representing voice; writers must choose what fits their intentions and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of prescriptive 'back-seat driving' advice from others. Know your audience and trust your instincts about the voice you want to create. Different aims (authenticity, readability, experimentation) justify different approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Is immersiveness important to you? (immersion vs detachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you want readers to be immersed (dream/hypnotised) or detached (made to think) by your use of dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy decoding (faithful transliteration) causes detachment because readers must use cognitive effort; subtler cues support immersion. Some writers deliberately disrupt immersion (Brechtian techniques) to provoke thought. Consider whether glossing unusual words is necessary and how it affects immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decision checklist: audience, clarity, immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask practical questions before choosing how to render voice and dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions offered: Who’s your audience? Who do you want to reach and why? Can you achieve your goals with rhythm and colour rather than heavy transliteration? If using unusual words, are they clear in context or do they need glossing (which may distract)? Use these to guide the balance between authenticity and readability.
